register read/management contracts are in Runtime and Persistence. Confirm bounds,
period buckets, ordering and cursors in the installed signatures. Build dimensions
and resources consistently with declared metadata. Changing schema after records
exist may be rejected; document the supported migration instead of suppressing
the engine's schema-drift check.

Acceptance must independently assert balances/turnovers or current reference
state, original history, retry behavior and reversal results. Test two competing
operations, failure rollback and a batch larger than one page. Measure provider
query counts and compare results across page boundaries; a unit test of a builder
does not establish transactional correctness or projection performance.

The [equipment usage example](../examples/equipment-inspection/README.md#equipment-usage-and-operational-registers)
contains an application document, Post validator, operational-register handler,
provider reader, migration and explicit Setup command. Its tests exercise actual
movement history, retry, Repost, Unpost, rollback after a write, and monthly
projection reads with two equipment dimensions. The shared Effects page displays
the public API result. Monthly projection tests invoke the finalizer explicitly;
this is not evidence of a scheduled worker or a volume/performance profile.

The [equipment assessment example](../examples/equipment-inspection/README.md#equipment-assessments-and-reference-registers)
implements a nonperiodic Reference Register subordinate to a document. Its handler
emits records for Post/Repost and leaves Unpost to the engine's recorder tombstones.
Read calls supply the recorder ID and paginate history/current keys using the
returned cursors. This does not implement a global latest-state register across
documents. Reference-register dimension IDs must correspond to
`DeterministicGuid.Create("Dimension|" + normalizedDimensionCode)`; use the same
value in the migration and runtime metadata, not an arbitrary UUID.

## Operational-register administration and health

`IOperationalRegisterAdminEndpoint` provides JSON-friendly metadata, physical
health and finalization operations. It is a trusted runtime facade: its name does
not imply current-user authorization. An interactive host must establish its
existing authorized boundary before invoking it. The reference application tests
these services directly and does not expose a new administration endpoint.

Inspect register list/details and the health of movement, turnover and balance
tables, including missing columns/indexes and the movement append-only guard.
Unknown register details/health/ensure return null. Ensuring physical schema does
not create movements. Use `EnsurePhysicalSchemasByIdsAsync` on the maintenance
service for targeted setup: the default batch implementation deduplicates IDs,
ignores empty/unknown IDs and leaves unrelated registers untouched. The extension
also supports non-batch implementations by calling them individually; do not
assume every custom implementation has the default batch normalization.

Read finalization markers using month-start periods and bounded limits. Dirty
months can be finalized per register or across registers; already finalized work
does not count again. The standard provider includes a default projector for new
registers. `BlockedNoProjector` is a defensive state for a host missing both an
applicable custom projector and the default registration, not the normal state
of every newly created register. After repairing that host configuration, explicitly
mark blocked months Dirty before retrying. Do not delete or edit marker tables.

## Transactional resource nets

Use `IOperationalRegisterResourceNetReader` when a trusted operation needs current
resource nets inside its existing unit-of-work transaction. It supports one or
several dimension-set IDs, one dimensional filter, and a batch of independent
dimensional filters with an inclusive as-of date. The batch filter result preserves
input order; missing matches yield zero. Set-ID batches deduplicate their IDs.
Specify a registered resource column code; do not derive identifiers from user
text. Empty filter groups and unknown resource columns are rejected.

These reads account for storno and do not require a preceding monthly finalization.
They are not permission-aware APIs. The
[administration and net-read example](../examples/equipment-inspection/README.md#operational-register-administration-and-nets)
verifies selective/idempotent schema ensure, default and missing-projector states,
bounded administration calls and two equipment dimensions with independent nets.
It posts 4 and 5 hours through HTTP, then unposts one 2.5-hour document and verifies
1.5 and 5 through all four net-read methods. Historical bounds exclude later
movements. This small functional fixture does not establish load/query-count or
concurrent-finalization performance.

## Dimension net pages and movement history

`IOperationalRegisterMovementsQueryReader` serves trusted reporting/read-side
operations. Its month-window resource nets and cumulative balances group by one
dimension value. Both require month-start `DateOnly` bounds, omit zero nets and
account for appended storno. Positive nets precede negative nets, with value UUID
ordering within each group. Rows include the value's display text. Offset pages
carry the filtered row count, positive sum and absolute negative sum; in the
default provider an empty offset page has zero totals, so do not replace previously
known totals with those of an out-of-range page.

For cumulative balances, prefer `GetResourceBalancesByDimensionCursorAsync` for
continuation. Start with a null cursor and use `HasMore`. Construct the next
`OperationalRegisterDimensionResourceNetCursor` from the last row's sign and
`ValueId`, the consumed row count, and the returned totals. The default PostgreSQL
provider seeks by sign/value and carries the first page's totals; the interface's
fallback implementation uses `NextOffset`. These are trusted continuation values,
not an authenticated HTTP cursor or a consistent snapshot across concurrent
writes. Restart paging if the register, resource, grouping dimension, filter or
month changes. An interactive adapter must enforce access and validate/bind its
own continuation data.

Cumulative reads can combine a finalized balance snapshot with later movements;
they also work before finalization. Bounded materialized helpers are suitable only
for known small results. Explicit pages avoid depending on their materialization
ceiling. The independent test compares movement-only, snapshot-plus-roll-forward
and fully finalized results, including negative values and a zero after reversal.

Movement history has two distinct time/order contracts. `GetByOccurredAtPageAsync`
and `GetByOccurredAtCursorAsync` accept inclusive exact UTC dates and order by
occurrence time, then movement ID. Carry both fields in
`OperationalRegisterOccurredAtCursor`; several records can share one timestamp.
The cursor method returns rows without `HasMore`: an adapter can request one
extra row, display its bounded page and continue from the last displayed row.
Use a bounded limit; a null offset-page limit explicitly disables paging.
In SDK 3.4.0, a null cursor starts the first bounded occurrence page. Continue
from the last displayed row's time and movement ID; no sentinel timestamp/ID
or offset-page workaround is needed. PostgreSQL parameters have explicit types,
including for the first request. See
[`operational-registers.null-occurrence-cursor`](../known-limitations.json).
`GetByMonthsAsync` instead requires month-start bounds and seeks by movement ID,
with optional dimension-set, document and storno filters. `GetMaxPeriodMonthAsync`
returns the latest matching month or null when there are no matching facts or
the registered table is not present. Dimension filters use AND semantics.

The [dimension paging example](../examples/equipment-inspection/README.md#operational-register-dimension-paging)
verifies equal-time continuation, exact-date bounds, differing month/occurrence
ordering, enriched dimensions, bounded pages, retained storno and maximum-month
filters. Its signed facts are seeded through the public technical applier against
real catalog/document records in disposable storage. This isolates reader
semantics; it does not establish an interactive posting rule, user authorization,
large-volume performance or concurrent-snapshot consistency.

## Reference-register administration and health

`IReferenceRegisterAdminEndpoint` exposes list/details and physical-schema health
through stable runtime DTOs. Like the operational-register facade, it is trusted
infrastructure and does not establish current-user authorization. Keep interactive
access behind the application's existing authorized boundary.

Health reports compare the records table, expected fields/indexes and append-only
guard with the registered metadata. Unknown register details/health/ensure return
null. Use `EnsurePhysicalSchemasByIdsAsync` for selected registers; the default
batch implementation deduplicates IDs and skips empty/unknown IDs. An adapter
without the batch interface instead receives individual calls from the extension,
so custom implementations must define their own normalization.

Normal management `UpsertAsync` ensures the table immediately. The
[administration example](../examples/equipment-inspection/README.md#reference-register-administration)
uses public persistence ports to model interrupted setup with metadata but no table.
For independent and subordinate nonperiodic registers, it verifies diagnosis,
selective ensure, repeated ensure and whole-report consistency without creating
records. This fixture does not claim every periodic index variant, damaged-schema
repair case or performance bound. Do not repair register storage with ad hoc SQL.

## Register-specific month projectors

Register a scoped `IOperationalRegisterMonthProjector` through host composition.
Its `RegisterCodeNorm` identifies the register; the runner trims and lowercases
that value and rejects empty or duplicate normalized codes. A matching custom
projector takes precedence over the default. Other registers retain the standard
fallback. Legacy `IOperationalRegisterMonthFinalizer` is adapted by the runner;
new extensions should use the projector interface.

`RebuildMonthAsync` receives registered identity, month-start period, UTC execution
time and a movement reader in `OperationalRegisterMonthProjectionContext`. A
transaction is already active. Use the same scoped unit of work and injected
provider-neutral projection stores. Do not begin a separate transaction, commit
the runner's transaction, or publish external side effects from this hook.
Use bounded reads and define the resource and cumulative-balance semantics of a
custom aggregation explicitly.

The runner publishes the Finalized marker only after the projector succeeds.
An exception rolls back its owned transaction, including changes to projections,
and preserves Dirty state. Callers who explicitly supply an external transaction
remain responsible for its rollback. A custom projector can delegate to
`IOperationalRegisterDefaultMonthProjector` when retaining standard aggregation.
The default's optional preparation path has additional transaction/lock conditions;
it is not automatically used for a register with a custom projector.

`CustomOperationalRegisterProjectorTests` posts 2 hours, verifies the custom hook
and default fallback for another register, then posts 1.5 more hours. An injected
failure after projection writes preserves the earlier 2-hour result and Dirty
marker; a subsequent successful run publishes 3.5 hours. Unposting the first
document leaves 1.5 hours. These are real provider transactions, with no sleeps
or test retries. The test deliberately delegates aggregation to the standard
projector; it does not claim a new aggregation algorithm or load certification.

The packaged `MovementsCountProjector` is a separate demonstration that requires
a `movement_count` resource. It publishes monthly net counts into both tables;
it is not a generic cumulative-balance implementation and is not registered by
default. Trusted finalization services are maintenance boundaries, not substitutes
for current-user authorization at an interactive endpoint.

# Application delivery and platform package boundaries

Build an independent application with exact, aligned SDK/UI/CLI/Kit versions.
Keep the resolved lockfiles and declared package sources reviewable. Use only
published registry artifacts or the explicitly selected sealed local candidate.
The npm CLI and application-template CLI have one implementation; a second
tooling template or a source checkout is not required.

`validate --profile build` and `test --profile all` execute development tooling.
They do not publish images, packages or deploy a service. Certification readiness
depends on every required gate and exact source/artifact identities, including
applicable performance and real-agent evidence for the Kit release itself.
Do not reuse a passing report after relevant inputs change.

Application deployment remains a separate operation. Review the target, secrets,
TLS/identity configuration, health checks, migration sequence and tested consistent
backup. The existing `deploy --backup-confirmed` flag asserts that backup condition;
it does not create a backup or establish authorization to publish a platform package.

For SDK/Kit changes, use the [coordinated upgrade workflow](upgrades.md). Preserve
application-owned code, configuration and custom guidance. A file rollback does
not reverse a database migration. Test the supported persisted upgrade and recovery
procedure before applying it to a deployment.

# Reporting, datasets, paging and exports

Target: NGB 3.4.0. Public contracts live in
[application services](contracts/NGB.Platform.Application.Abstractions.json),
[Contracts](contracts/NGB.Platform.Contracts.json),
[Runtime](contracts/NGB.Platform.Runtime.json) and
[Persistence](contracts/NGB.Platform.Persistence.json).

Choose between a canonical report's supported extension and a composable dataset.
Use `IReportDefinitionSource` for report definitions and
`IReportDefinitionEnricher` for static changes to those definitions. Read the
assembled catalog through `IReportDefinitionProvider`.
`IReportDatasetSource.GetDatasets()` supplies dataset metadata; metadata alone
does not implement bounded data execution. `IReportMetadataContributor` is a
separate public declaration that the current standard catalog does not consume.
Implementing it alone does not change `/api/report-definitions`; use the active
definition-enricher composition described below.

`IReportPageDataSource.ReadPageAsync(ReportDataQuery, ReportPlanPaging,
ReportRowSelection?, CancellationToken)` supplies provider-neutral bounded reads
at the requested aggregation grain. A row selection is a bounded union of keys;
apply it with one set-based query, not one query per selected row. Keep SQL in the
provider project, use parameterized inputs and enforce supported filter/sort fields.

`IReportSpecializedPlanExecutor` identifies its ReportCode and participates in the
shared planning/rendering path. Its `PrepareExecution` resolves time-dependent
defaults once per attempt; `ExecuteAsync` returns a `ReportDataPage`. It is not
permission to bypass report admission, authorization or paging limits. For
streaming and download paths, inspect `IStreamingReportDataSource`,
`IStreamingReportExportService` and `IReportDownloadService` separately.

Use `IAuthorizedReportReadService` for current-user integrations. Report variants
also have their own access-context contract; UI hiding alone is insufficient.
In an HTTP host register `IReportVariantAccessContext` with the public
`HttpReportVariantAccessContext` after Runtime registration. The Runtime default
has no actor, so enabling `AllowsVariants` in metadata alone cannot save a private
variant. The HTTP adapter uses the real current actor and the SDK projects the
owner into platform users when needed, including an unlinked Keycloak administrator.
Do not substitute a fixed actor or use an editable role display name.

`ReportControllerBase` supplies `/api/reports/{reportCode}/variants`. Private
variants are scoped to their owner; identical codes may belong to different users.
Shared variants require `ManageSharedVariants` to change. Saving one's own variant
uses `SavePrivateVariant`; deletion uses `DeleteVariant` or management permission.
Read operations still require report access. A default is unique within its private
owner or shared scope. Do not use the same code for private and shared variants:
that collision is rejected. Route identity takes precedence over body identity.
Use `ReportVariantLimits` for name, code and payload limits. Saving JSON does not
prove every requested layout/filter is executable; execution validates the saved
request against the report definition. Test that execution separately.
Use public shared UI components/exports for rendering and drilldown rather than
private framework source imports.

Freeze expected rows, totals and group subtotals before implementing the query.
Test empty data, multiple pages, boundary keys, tied sort values, invalid/stale
cursors, unauthorized dimensions, changed snapshots and export cancellation.
Reconcile total counts across paging and export; verify that filters applied to
visible rows also constrain totals. Measure actual query count and bounded memory.

## Parameters and authorization test setup

For the standard PostgreSQL composable path, supply `from_utc`, `to_utc` and
`as_of_utc` as strict ISO `yyyy-MM-dd` dates. The provider converts inclusive
upper dates to exclusive next-day bounds. Upper dates must therefore be earlier
than `9999-12-31`; a lower date can use the entire supported date range.
Malformed or unrepresentable upper dates produce `report.layout.invalid`, a
`parameters.<code>` field path and HTTP 400. This validation applies to ordinary,
paged and streaming execution. A parameter marked `IsRequired` must be present.
Other date parameters still need validation in their executor; declaring date
metadata alone does not establish it. Actual SDK configuration failures retain
their original error classification.

Use a distinct test identity for an ungranted reader, a display-name-only
administrator and a registered application administrator. Link roles before each
identity's first request. The example's `InspectionHost.LinkUserAsync` performs
initial repository setup; repeating it after a request does not implement the
public role-change workflow or invalidate cached permissions. For intentional
role changes, use the public security API as demonstrated by
`SecurityAdministrationHttpTests`. Keep the inactive-account assertion after
the successful administrator request. See [verification guidance](testing.md).

`InspectionReportTests` demonstrates these independent actors and separately
verifies malformed-date HTTP 400 responses and parameter field paths. Parameterize negative HTTP cases or
include the request identity in assertions so a failure identifies its input.

## Composable example

The [equipment inspection example](../examples/equipment-inspection/README.md#inspection-summary)
supplies a composable report through `IReportDefinitionSource` and
`IReportDatasetSource`. Its provider uses `IPostgresReportDatasetSource` and
`PostgresReportDatasetBinding`, leaving paging and XLSX streaming to the shared
engine. Use `Count` for a record count, including an empty selection; `Sum` has
different empty-set semantics. The example verifies grouping, filters, cursors,
exported values and authorization. It does not establish support for every report
shape, pivots or workload performance. `ReportVariantHttpTests` checks two owners,
shared mutation denial, independent private codes, default replacement, route
identity, unchanged data after invalid writes and execution of a saved filter.

`ReportStreamingTests` reads 501 actual Posted inspections through
`IStreamingReportDataSource` in a real `IReportReadSession`. For this SDK version
the provider returns batches of at most 500 rows. A write from another HTTP
request after the first fetch is invisible to the active snapshot and visible to
the next session. Cancellation after the first batch is followed by
`EndAsync(CancellationToken.None)` in `finally`: cleanup must not reuse the cancelled
token. The test checks that no transaction remains active and that the same scoped
provider can read again. An empty selection also completes. These are trusted
provider contracts, not authorized public HTTP endpoints. The interactive report
and export boundaries retain their own permission checks. This proves bounded
fetching and cancellation for this query, not a measured process-wide memory limit.

For a fixed report shape, `InspectionOutcomeReportDefinition` and
`InspectionOutcomeReportExecutor` demonstrate `IReportSpecializedPlanExecutor`.
The canonical `example.inspection-outcome-rate` report returns one prebuilt row:
total Posted inspections, those with the exact result `Passed`, and their percentage.
Its two provider aggregates each return one row inside the shared report read
session. The executor performs arithmetic on those scalar counts, not in-memory
aggregation of documents. Empty input returns zero counts and an undefined
percentage, displayed as `No inspections`.

Register the definition source and scoped specialized executor through the public
interfaces. Keep the default layout consistent with declared capabilities:
`ReportLayoutDto` enables totals by default, so a report that disables that option
must specify it explicitly. This fixed shape does not advertise variants, filters,
grouping or XLSX export. HTTP tests verify 3/5 = 60%, Draft exclusion, period
selection, empty input, shared request validation, both administrator forms,
denied readers, inactive accounts and cancellation. A specialized executor remains
behind `IAuthorizedReportReadService`; calling it directly is trusted service code.

For the four built-in financial statements, follow the
[accounting workflow](accounting.md#built-in-financial-statements). Their canonical
root pages can return group headers and grand totals; read account children with
the returned `ChildrenPath` as the next request's `GroupPath`. A group header is
not evidence that its account detail has already been materialized in that page.

The [built-in ledger workflow](accounting.md#built-in-ledger-and-diagnostic-reports)
also distinguishes grouped Ledger Analysis from its flat cursor mode. Default
account headers have empty measure cells when subtotals use separate rows.
Use row kinds and column codes to locate values. Trial Balance's Debit/Credit
columns report turnover, while Account Card and General Ledger expose running
balances for the selected account.


## Trusted persistence contracts behind built-in reports

Built-in reports use specialized page, stream and snapshot ports in
`NGB.Persistence.Readers.Reports`. Their public signatures describe provider data,
not an authorized interactive endpoint. Keep HTTP/MCP use behind
`IAuthorizedReportReadService`, and retain the report read session when consuming
streams. A snapshot DTO describes its aggregated values and projection provenance;
it does not by itself open or hold a transaction.

The canonical Account Card consumes the effective page/stream readers, including
its opening balance and range totals. The separate raw Account Card ports have
different reduction semantics and are not interchangeable with that path.
General Ledger snapshots carry opening/range totals; Trial Balance has distinct
account-only and account/dimension row grains. Shared `AccountingSummary` pages
carry section/account values and explicit keyset continuation for Trial Balance,
Balance Sheet, Income Statement and Equity. Consistency pages/streams carry
read-only comparison results and diagnostics, not storage repair commands.

These supporting contracts are checked against the exact packaged signatures and
the existing report pipeline. The independent report scenarios verify their
public business results. That evidence does not certify a replacement database
provider, every low-level query shape or unbounded materialization. Use explicit
pages/streams and the existing bounded readers for application-specific work.

## Definition enrichment and execution boundaries

Register `IReportDefinitionEnricher` contributors when an application needs to
adjust an existing report's static presentation or filter metadata. The standard
catalog applies them in registration order while assembling its definitions.
Return unrelated definitions unchanged and preserve `ReportCode`; replacing that
identity fails catalog construction. Keep enrichers independent of the current
request, actor and mutable per-request state. `ReportDefinitionEnrichmentTests`
registers two contributors, checks their composed HTTP metadata and unaffected
reports, and verifies that reader authorization still applies.

The public report contracts serve different boundaries:

| Contract family | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| `IReportDefinitionSource`, `IReportDatasetSource`, `IReportDefinitionEnricher` | Application-owned definition contributions. |
| `IAuthorizedReportReadService`, concrete authenticated `ReportControllerBase` subclass | User-facing definition and execution access. The controller also checks export and variant mutation permissions. |
| `IReportEngine`, `IReportPlanExecutor`, `ITabularReportPlanExecutor` | Trusted execution and dispatch after the appropriate access boundary. |
| `Application.Abstractions.Services.ReportPlan*`, `ReportDataColumn`, `ReportExecutionResult` | Provider-neutral query and result shapes. |
| `Runtime.Reporting.Planning.ReportPlan*`, `ReportQueryPlan`, normalized runtime models | Intermediate planning and rendering representations, produced by the standard engine. |
| `PostgresReportExecution*`, selection records, SQL statement/cursor metadata | Persistence-owned query compilation and results. SQL and aliases stay server-owned. |
| `IReportVariantRepository`, `ReportVariantRecord` | Trusted variant persistence; a caller-supplied user ID does not establish authentication. |
| `IReportDownload`, `IStreamingReportExportService` | Single-use download lifetime and forward-only worksheet output. Dispose the download even after cancellation. |

Prefer the existing definition, dataset and specialized-executor interfaces when
extending reports. Similar type names across runtime and provider namespaces do
not make their models interchangeable. These contract references do not certify
an alternative provider or every possible grouping/pivot shape.

## Per-host admission and continuation keys

`AddInfrastructure` binds `Reporting:Requests`. Configure page and XLSX download
capacity independently through `ConcurrentPages`, `QueuedPages`,
`ConcurrentDownloads` and `QueuedDownloads`. The corresponding queue deadlines
are `PageQueueTimeoutSeconds` and `DownloadQueueTimeoutSeconds`; execution
deadlines are `PageTimeoutSeconds` and `DownloadTimeoutSeconds`. Concurrency and
deadlines must be positive; queues may be zero. Startup validation rejects
negative queues and timeouts beyond the cancellation timer range.

The standard report controller applies the shared `ReportRequestBudget`. A busy
capacity/queue returns HTTP 429 with `Retry-After`; releasing the execution lease
admits later requests. Other transports can use `IReportRequestAdmission` for
the same page capacity, dispose the acquired lease and retain their authorized
report service. Do not acquire a second lease around an HTTP controller action
that already has the budget filter. Limits apply to each running host, not to an
entire deployment or a particular user's business permissions.

`ReportAdmissionTests` exercises real authenticated page and XLSX endpoints while
each capacity is occupied, verifies independent capacity and recovery, and checks
queued cancellation without sleeps. It does not establish workload throughput or
exercise execution-deadline expiry.

Set `Reporting:Cursor:SigningKey` through the application's secret configuration
to Base64 of at least 32 cryptographically random bytes. Instances that should
accept each other's continuations need the same key. Without this setting the
process creates an ephemeral key, so another process or a restart cannot verify
its continuations. Replacing the key invalidates existing continuations; users
must run the report again. This HMAC protects integrity, not confidentiality, and
does not replace report authorization or query-fingerprint validation.

The example verifies configuration binding, a second protector with the same
key and rejection with a different key. Existing HTTP paging checks verify
tampered and changed-query continuation rejection. Together they validate these
contracts, not a deployed multi-instance topology or an automated rotation scheme.

## Explicit dimension scope expansion

An `IReportDimensionScopeExpander` can expand an explicitly requested dimension
selection using application-owned relationships. Register it through standard DI
and declare `SupportsIncludeDescendants: true` in the report's filter/field
metadata. The lookup metadata must identify the registered catalog dimension or
a single document dimension. The flag alone does not create hierarchy semantics;
a registered contributor alone does not enable descendant requests.

`IDimensionDefinitionReader` resolves active registered dimension codes to IDs.
`IDimensionScopeExpansionService` composes contributors in registration order;
each receives the previous result. Select the intended report and dimension,
preserve unrelated scopes, propagate cancellation and bound relationship lookups.
Null and empty input scopes bypass contributors. Values within one dimension
form an OR selection, while multiple dimensions form an AND selection.

The standard report adapter requests expansion for explicit IncludeDescendants
filters, converts the result back into value filters and clears that flag for
execution. It rejects more than 5000 expanded values. Do not use this post-expansion
check as permission to perform an unbounded traversal inside your contributor.
Continue through the authorized report service; the composition service itself
is trusted server code and performs no user access check.

`ReportDimensionScopeTests` uses an explicit four-equipment fixture: two ordered
contributors expand one selected equipment to its child and grandchild, producing
three posted inspections while excluding the fourth. A direct selection returns
one, an unrelated selection remains unchanged, and a denied reader never invokes
the contributors. Other cases verify the metadata opt-in, cancellation and the
expanded-value limit with subsequent recovery. This establishes extension wiring
and bounded HTTP behavior, not a built-in catalog hierarchy or workload throughput.

## Built-in executor implementation boundaries

Canonical helpers parse ISO dates, normalize accounting periods, validate bounded
GUID selections and reserve page space for summary rows. Materialized execution
keeps an overflow probe so an overlarge result fails instead of silently returning
a partial report. These helpers do not replace report authorization, admission
limits or registered dimension expansion.

Accounting summary and consistency page executors use internal continuation
positions; specialized cursor encoding alone is not a signature. The report
service owns the protected, request-bound cursor envelope. Built-in financial
statement streaming executors serialize trusted prepared execution state and
render ordered accounts into details, sections and totals. Prepared JSON is not
a user permission token. Standard export authorization and resource limits remain
required. Account-card cell actions describe navigation; the destination still
checks access when opened.

## Custom streaming export executor

Register one scoped `IStreamingReportExecutor` for an exact report code to
specialize XLSX export; the `"*"` executor remains the standard fallback. Duplicate
matching executors are invalid. `Prepare` receives the resolved variant/filter
request and must freeze required inputs. `ReadAsync` runs in the report read
session and must honor cancellation. Emit each row exactly once with consecutive
zero-based ordinals. `Template` must be available after the first read, including
an empty stream. Do not retain a requesting user's mutable state in a singleton.

The HTTP report controller performs authorization and export capability checks;
calling the low-level download service directly is trusted orchestration. Keep
`IReportDownload` disposed after success, failure or cancellation so its read
session and transaction are released. It can be written only once. Errors before
the first row can fail before response headers; later streaming errors cannot be
reported as a complete successful download.

`ReportStreamingExtensionTests` uses synthetic rows to verify exact executor
selection, refusal before preparation, failure before the first row, recovery,
frozen parameters, single-write behavior and cleanup after cancellation. It tests
the extension lifecycle, not new business calculations or export throughput.

## Time fields and drill-down

A `ReportFieldDto` declaring `SupportedTimeGrains` must have
`Kind: ReportFieldKind.Time`, not `Dimension`, and a supported date/time data type.
Construct the actual dataset definition and execute the report endpoint during
acceptance; this configuration error can fail before SQL is executed.
For each advertised grain, the `PostgresReportFieldBinding` must also supply its
matching bucket expression (for example `monthBucketSqlExpression`). The provider
does not derive those expressions from field metadata. Enable `AllowsDetailFields`
and `AllowsShowDetails` when the report exposes selectable detail rows, and test
both a time-grouped request and a detail request through HTTP.

Every report has a meaningful detail path. For composable entity references use
`<prefix>_display` plus `<prefix>_id`, with the ID field declaring the appropriate
`CatalogLookupSourceDto` or single-type `DocumentLookupSourceDto`. Include the
supporting ID value in the selected row; a display string named `customer` or
`document` alone is not a navigation target. The built-in `document_display` and
`account_display` paths use their specific `ReportInteractiveSupport` fields;
inspect their installed contract rather than guessing support-column names.

Grouped figures must drill to the contributing details with the same period,
filters and authorization. Detail rows must open the source record/document.
Use the public composable action support or the report executor's declared cell
and row actions. Test returned actions and browser clicks, not just nonempty
metadata or a filter dialog. Never attach a link to an arbitrary representative
record as the drill-down for an aggregate.

Detail capabilities and lookup metadata enable source navigation; they do not
automatically create an aggregate-to-details action for an arbitrary grouping.
Compose that action through a supported report executor, carrying the selected
group as a filter and the detail layout into the destination report. Verify both
steps separately; source links alone do not prove grouped drill-down.

Enumerate registered report definitions and execute every one through the
permission-aware HTTP endpoint with valid required parameters. Use nonempty known
data, empty selections and boundary periods; verify rows, totals, paging and
supported export. Keep required per-report inputs explicit. Direct SQL sums and
dashboard tests are complementary reconciliation, not report execution tests.

# Identity, permissions and feature flags

Target: NGB 3.4.0. Public contracts:
[Runtime](contracts/NGB.Platform.Runtime.json),
[ASP.NET hosting](contracts/NGB.Platform.Hosting.AspNetCore.json),
[application services](contracts/NGB.Platform.Application.Abstractions.json).

Keycloak settings establish issuer, metadata endpoint and allowed client IDs.
Production metadata uses HTTPS; loopback HTTP is limited to disposable tests.
Keep secrets in the configured secret store/environment, never in instructions,
versioned settings, prompts or evidence. Use the starter's authentication wiring.

`INgbPermissionDefinitionSource` contributes permission definitions.
`INgbAccessChecker.RequireAsync(resourceKind, resourceCode, actionCode,
CancellationToken)` enforces a capability; `HasAsync` supports availability
queries. Record-level authorization and feature prerequisites still apply.
Reuse the public authorized application services instead of exposing raw readers.

Configure explicit application administrator role codes through
`NgbAdministratorOptions.ApplicationRoleCodes`. Active administrators receive all
registered capabilities without manual grants. Trusted Keycloak `ngb-admin` also
works before a platform user exists. Editable role names are never authority.
Inactive accounts stay blocked. Optional feature flags remain independent of
permissions. Personal state may require a linked platform user: the starter tests
verify that unlinked administrators can manage roles while personal Work Center
state retains its existing linked-user prerequisite.

Test anonymous, insufficient permission, active application administrator, trusted
Keycloak administrator without a platform record, inactive identity and disabled
feature separately. For each UI action, assert the corresponding backend result.
Changing a permission display name must not change access. Newly contributed
permissions must be accessible to existing administrators without adding grants.

## User and role administration

Expose the existing `SecurityControllerBase` from an authorized application
controller. It checks `NgbSystemPermissions` before invoking trusted
`IUserAccessManagementService` and `IRoleManagementService` operations. Those
services do not replace the caller's authorization boundary.

User creation links or creates an identity-provider user, then persists the platform
record, assignments and provisioning operation. Updates retain that identity;
deactivation/reactivation update both platform and identity-provider state.
Configure `KeycloakAdminClientSettings` separately from token validation: base URL,
realm and a confidential client with only the required realm user-management roles.
The starter realm permits username editing because the existing admin client uses
email as username when updating a profile. Keep the client secret outside source.

Role and assignment changes update access versions and audit evidence. Read current
access through `/api/security/me/access`; administrator reads of another user's
effective access retain the defined resource groups, with empty `Actions` for
resources the user cannot access. An empty permission set does not imply an empty
group list. User-list cursors bind the active-status filter and use bounded pages.

Registered administrator roles remain protected: applications may rename their
display labels, but cannot replace their reserved code, deactivate the role or
replace its implicit full-access permissions with explicit grants. Ordinary roles
support creation, updates, permission replacement and activation through the public
API. Preserve the distinction between role state and the user's active state.

`SecurityAdministrationHttpTests` in the independent example exercises these routes
against disposable PostgreSQL and Keycloak instances. It covers both administrator
kinds, user/profile/role lifecycle, access-version changes, audit records, cursor
filter binding and refusal for ungranted, inactive or anonymous callers.

## Identity and administration data

`ActorIdentity` comes from the trusted execution host. Its external subject and
roles describe an authenticated context; constructing the record does not
authenticate a request. `DisplayName` is presentation data. Continue to resolve
registered application administrator role codes and the trusted `ngb-admin` role
through the standard services, retaining active-account checks.

`IdentityProviderUserDto` and `IdentityProviderUserBatch` are administration
projections, not permission snapshots. Create/update requests belong behind the
authorized user-management workflow; keep temporary passwords out of diagnostics,
audit metadata and Kit files. A page snapshot reader must use its in-process
projection/cache and must not issue one remote identity-provider call per row.

Deployment `NgbFeatureDefinition` metadata stays independent of these identities
and permissions. An administrator grant does not enable a disabled feature.

# Verification profiles and evidence

Use the application's own `node infrastructure/ngb.mjs` entry point. `doctor`,
plain `validate`, `ai status` and sync preview inspect configuration/data without
executing application builds or tests. `validate --profile build` executes trusted
project tooling and inspects resolved dependencies and managed metadata.

`test` defaults to unit tests. `test --profile integration` runs backend integration
suites; `test --profile e2e` runs browser workflows; `test --profile all` requires
unit, integration and browser suites. Required missing/skipped checks fail.
Unit tests include frontend browser-component prerequisites where configured.
The CLI collects backend TRX/Cobertura and frontend/browser discovery evidence.

For the official starter, the combined backend gate requires every compiled
production source to appear and achieve 100% lines, branches and methods. The
frontend requires 100% lines, branches, functions and statements per file. Only
audited declaration/generated-code exclusions apply. Do not remove discovered
files, suppress a reachable branch or accept an empty report to reach a threshold.

Use `.ngb/reports/<run-id>/report.json` and its referenced report hashes. Source
inputs must remain unchanged during a run. Record actual suite counts and failures;
passing a build does not prove startup, data migration or business correctness.

Child tools receive an isolated environment with explicit runtime paths and
caches. Standard `HTTP_PROXY`, `HTTPS_PROXY`, `ALL_PROXY`, `NO_PROXY` and lowercase
equivalents are retained for network transport. Proxy URLs must be bounded origins
without paths, queries or fragments; HTTP(S) is supported, and `ALL_PROXY` also
accepts SOCKS5/SOCKS5H. Embedded proxy authentication is accepted only for the
loopback hosts `localhost`, `127.0.0.1` and `[::1]`, for native sandbox transport.
Proxy user/password values are redacted from subprocess diagnostics. `NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=1` is retained only
when a nonempty proxy is present. Separate API tokens, deployment connections
and package-registry overrides are not inherited. Proxy settings do not replace
the evaluator's native network restrictions or authorize access to a deployment.
An agent sandbox may protect `.agents` even when ordinary application files are
writable. Installing/updating managed skills needs permission for the application
skill directories. Codex can use a scoped write grant for those directories.
Claude Code's native Bash sandbox protects `.claude/skills` even when `allowWrite`
covers it; that mode cannot commit a coordinated Kit upgrade. Run the reviewed
target CLI command from your own terminal when the client blocks this operation.
Do not disable the sandbox or grant access to unrelated configuration just to
install skills. A failed upgrade must retain its error and transaction/recovery
evidence. See the clients' [filesystem permissions](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/permissions)
and [protected paths](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#protected-paths).

`certify --profile external-application` also requires its performance evidence;
an incomplete certification profile must report NOT READY.

Kit capability acceptance binds a declared source to its actual test runner and
raw report hash. Backend cases use the full TRX test name. Browser cases use a
canonical JSON array of the Playwright project name, any nested describe titles,
and the test title; the source path is checked separately against the packaged
example. An unnamed project uses an empty first string. Aggregate browser counts
alone cannot certify a named capability. Missing cases, another project, an
unpackaged file, changed reports, retries or skips cause refusal. A failing
independent example does not receive a passing capability certification.

The versioned `starter-http-v1` workload uses k6 1.2.2 against the owned test API.
Each of three repetitions warms up 20 iterations, then runs four virtual users
with 50 iterations each. Each iteration reads roles and the main menu as a test
administrator. Both routes must complete exactly 200 measured requests per
repetition, return successful JSON, have no failures and meet p95 below 500 ms and
p99 below 1000 ms. These initial budgets precede measurements; they are not a
historical comparison. `performance-plan.json` records the workload, hashes and
runner hardware before execution; per-repetition evidence records measured values.
This profile covers starter HTTP reads. Add separate acceptance and load workloads
for application business behavior, data volumes and query budgets.

Integration/E2E use test-only credentials and disposable services. The CLI owns
the browser environment and cleans it after success, failure or handled
cancellation. It verifies ownership before removing containers, networks or
volumes. Never attach an existing application database or use deployment `.env`.
Before provisioning, the CLI writes a private ownership receipt under
`.ngb/test-runs/<run-id>/`. After an abrupt controller kill, inspect
`node infrastructure/ngb.mjs recover --resources`, then use the same command with
`--apply` to remove that application's owned resources and staging files. Recovery
requires the original host and application path, and refuses live owner/provisioner
processes or mismatched Docker ownership. If the controller died before recording
the provisioner PID, inspect that process manually; recovery must not guess that
provisioning has stopped. A reused live PID also causes a conservative refusal.
Receipts contain no credentials; the private staging directory contains only
disposable test credentials and is removed with its resources.

Define business outcomes independently of implementation: known totals, version
conflicts, retries, rollback and unauthorized calls. Verify real API and provider
behavior before making persistence or security claims. Freeze performance workloads,
runner identity and tolerances before measuring them; separate tooling timings,
query counts, volume tests and live load results.

When a document gains a Post requirement, update the positive test data as well
as its new validation tests. The example's `InspectionRequests.CompleteInspectionPayload`
is the shared valid input for lifecycle, batch posting, reporting and typed-storage
guard tests; `CreateCompleteInspectionAsync` uses it too. Keep the generic
`Payload`, `PostAsync` and action helpers transparent: they must not silently add
fields that would conceal invalid input. Explicit incomplete Drafts, validation
cases and frozen migration-baseline records retain their own inputs.
Search all successful Post paths, including tests outside the document's named
test class, and run the affected regression classes. A guard or report test that
fails while creating its setup has not exercised the invariant it claims to test.

Compare JSON responses by values, not serialized text. An idempotent action replay
may read its stored result from PostgreSQL `jsonb`, which can reorder object
properties. Use `InspectionRequests.AssertEquivalentJsonAsync` or deserialize and
compare typed fields; `JsonElement.DeepEquals` ignores object property order while
still checking values, missing members and array order. Keep explicit assertions
for status, version and side effects. Do not require byte-for-byte response equality
unless the public contract explicitly promises it.

Create test identities and initial role links before their first request. To test
changing an existing user's access, use the public user/role management API: it
updates access versions as well as assignments. Direct repository setup does not
reproduce that invalidation contract after permissions have been cached. Prefer
separate fresh identities for independent positive/negative administrator cases,
and keep role codes unique within the test database. Administrator behavior must
still be based on registered codes, including after a display-name change.
`InspectionHost.LinkUserAsync` is initial setup, not a role-change API. The
report example uses different identities for a reader, a display-name-only
administrator and a registered administrator, then verifies deactivation on the
same administrator. Preserve that separation when adapting its tests.

Keep negative HTTP cases individually identifiable through parameterized tests or
an assertion message containing a synthetic case name. Derive expected statuses
from the installed public behavior rather than assuming all invalid inputs map
to 400. Record unsupported error mappings explicitly, as for
[composable report date parameters](reporting.md#parameters-and-authorization-test-setup).
Such a characterization test documents current behavior; it does not establish
that an unmet application requirement has been implemented.

Vitest Browser Mode uses native ESM caching. `vi.resetModules()` does not make a
second import of the same startup module execute its side effects again. For
bootstrap tests, import `startApplication` from `src/bootstrap.ts` and call/await
it for each case, including parameterized cases. The example and starter keep
`src/main.ts` as the one-time browser entry point and test that entry separately.
Use a pending promise only when proving an intermediate state such as waiting
for access loading; await completion before the test ends. Reset mock state per
test. Do not repair a missing second startup by increasing waits or by adding
arbitrary query strings to imports.

Give browser-created lookup records distinct names for each repeated scenario.
For a view-only editor, wait for the saved field value and assert that Save is
disabled. When checking API metadata during sign-in, register the response wait
before the triggering action and read the body before the next full-page
navigation. Chromium may discard the previous page's response body after
`page.goto()`. Pair a wait for an editor GET with the navigation that triggers it.
Keep exact-match selectors and assert both the displayed numeric value and the
saved API payload. If input is intermittent, retain the failing report and record
the affected field's input events; a successful repetition alone does not identify
the cause or turn the original failed candidate into a passing one.

# Ownership and upgrade rules

`ai/vendor/` and rendered `ngb-*` skills are official content. `ai/custom/`, custom
skill sources, project code, tests and `ngb.config.json` belong to the application.
Root `AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md` contain bounded NGB blocks; text outside them survives
byte-for-byte. Custom `app-*` adapters are generated from their canonical sources.

`ai sync` without `--to` uses the installed Kit. It does not discover a new release.
A different SDK version needs `upgrade --to <exact-version>`, which coordinates
SDK, UI, CLI and Kit changes. A new template installation does not rewrite an
existing application. Preview never writes application files or local caches.

Three-way comparison uses verified old bytes, local bytes and incoming bytes.
Unchanged files update; local-only changes remain customized. Changed upstream
content conflicting with local edits requires a decision. Local deletion is a
change. New official paths never implicitly adopt existing unowned files.

Resolution data has `schemaVersion: 1`, the preview's `planSha256`, and a `decisions`
array. Each decision contains its conflict `id` and `choice`: `local`, `incoming`
or `replacement`. A replacement also contains reviewed UTF-8/LF `content`.
Decisions are not executable hooks. Any input change invalidates the plan digest.
Keeping a customization does not prove that its required contracts still hold.

Applied changes retain a private recovery receipt under `.ngb/transactions/`.
An incomplete transaction blocks further writes until recovery is reviewed with
`node infrastructure/ngb.mjs recover`. Read [interrupted transactions](recovery.md)
before applying recovery; never delete its journal or lock to suppress a
diagnostic. Database migration and deployment remain separate, with the
established backup requirement.

## Accounting guard migration in 3.4.0

The platform migration `V2026_11_08_0100__accounting_posting_boundary.sql` replaces
ledger guards to reject writes before a later closed month. It preserves ledger
rows, turnovers, snapshots and closed-period markers. Run the target Migrator
before starting matching hosts, as for the RR migration below. A successful
migration does not certify that historical snapshots were already correct.
Previously affected periods require explicit review and authorized reopening/
closing, respecting fiscal-year dependencies. Keep Evolve ordering and checksum
validation enabled; an out-of-order error requires inspecting the migration
sequence, not globally enabling OutOfOrder.

## Reference-register migration in 3.4.0

Updating packages does not execute SQL. Update the application's Migrator together
with its API/workers, preserve a verified consistent backup, stop the old processes,
run the target Migrator, and start matching target hosts only after it succeeds.
The API and worker do not perform this migration at startup. Use a maintenance
window because the DDL acquires table locks; do not mix reader/writer versions.

The platform migration discovers periodic `SubordinateToRecorder` RR tables from
application metadata and adds `__is_recorder_cancellation boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT
false`. No per-application migration or standard handler change is required. New
registers receive the column through the normal schema service. A business-field
or unowned-column collision stops migration without overwriting application data.

Existing history and ordinary deletion meanings are preserved. Do not guess and
bulk-relabel old tombstones or claim old incorrect states were automatically
repaired. Investigate an affected document before an authorized lifecycle correction,
including any closed-period restrictions. Custom SQL depending on the entire row
shape and custom effective-state readers need review. Standard DTOs and business
field dictionaries do not expose the internal flag.

# Work Center, outbox and background jobs

Target: NGB 3.4.0. Inspect
[application services](contracts/NGB.Platform.Application.Abstractions.json),
[Definitions](contracts/NGB.Platform.Definitions.json),
[BackgroundJobs](contracts/NGB.Platform.BackgroundJobs.json) and
[Runtime](contracts/NGB.Platform.Runtime.json).

Use `IWorkCenterTaskService` and `INotificationService` to create supported task
and notification requests. Requests carry stable deduplication keys, source
references and correlation/causation identifiers. Notification recipients are
either explicit users or one role source, not both. Preserve that invariant.

`WorkCenterMutationResult` returns changed user IDs. Notify only after the
transaction commits; do not carry mutable scoped state across that boundary.
`IDocumentActionCompletedWorkCenterPolicy` reacts to the existing completion event.
`IOutboxProcessor.ProcessBatchAsync` processes bounded work; retry behavior must
preserve deduplication and avoid notifying about rolled-back changes.

`IWorkCenterQueryService` owns current-user list/summary, preferences and supported
read/claim/snooze/dismiss operations. Claims use an expected version. Use these
services and public UI exports; do not let an agent mutate task tables directly.

For Hangfire composition, explicit schedules, register finalization and runner
failure semantics, read [background jobs](background-jobs.md). Outbox delivery
and recurring jobs have distinct execution and retry contracts.

Verify repeated events, concurrent claims, role recipients, disabled preferences,
rollback before commit, retry after a partial failure, bounded batch sizes and
worker restart. Observe health and failed delivery counts. A scheduled job's
registration is not proof that its business effect actually ran.

## Retention and maintenance

`IWorkCenterMaintenanceService.PruneAsync` performs trusted, bounded maintenance.
Configure the existing `Ngb:WorkCenter` policy through `NgbWorkCenterOptions`:
completed action receipts default to 90 days, terminal tasks to 180 days,
notification deliveries and outbox records to 30 days. The default batch size is
1,000 with at most ten batches per invocation. The batch bound applies separately
to each candidate record kind; it is not a global maximum for all deleted rows.
Each batch runs in a transaction and a run stops early when nothing is removed.

Only completed action receipts are eligible by completion time. Expiring a receipt
allows its idempotency key to begin a new execution; choose retention to cover the
application's retry window. This does not delete the document or its business audit.
Completed/cancelled tasks expire by their last update; open tasks remain. Notification
deliveries age from dismissal or notification expiry. Old notification records
can disappear once no deliveries reference them; a later batch can collect them.

Outbox retention uses event creation time and preserves events with any Pending,
Processing or Failed consumer state. Completed and DeadLetter states are terminal
for retention. The latter are eligible for removal, so arrange operational review
within the configured retention window. This maintenance contract does not provide
a manual redrive API. Public cutoff/result DTOs and the maintenance repository
describe provider work; they do not establish current-user authorization.

`WorkCenterMaintenanceTests` uses a controlled `TimeProvider`, disposable PostgreSQL
and the actual public runtime/provider. Four cases check expired/recent/unfinished
receipts, bounded task deletion, live notification preservation and outbox terminal
states. No wall-clock waits or manual SQL are required. These tests do not claim
deployment scheduler or configuration-binding coverage.

## Tasks, delivery and preferences in an external application

The [HTTP contract example](../examples/equipment-inspection/EquipmentInspection.IntegrationTests/WorkCenterHttpTests.cs)
registers test-owned `IWorkCenterPreferenceDefinitionSource` definitions and
creates synthetic work through trusted public application services. Its read and
mutation assertions use the actual `WorkCenterControllerBase` endpoints and
Keycloak identities. These service tests are separate from the application-owned
withdrawal policy described below. There is no generic notification-creation endpoint.

A Work Center user needs an active linked platform identity. Administration does
not imply a personal Work Center identity exists. Task assignment and notification
delivery choose recipients separately from source visibility: a recipient without
view permission for the source cannot list or mark that item read. The source
reference preserves kind, code and entity ID; it is not permission to read them.

`CreateWorkCenterTaskRequest` requires exactly one user or role assignment. A
role-assigned open task can be claimed with its expected version; competing
claims have one winner. Reading and snoozing affect personal attention state.
Completion/cancellation use the public task service and stable deduplication keys;
repeating a terminal operation does not report another change. Task completion
does not itself execute a document action.

In-app notification delivery is deduplicated per definition/key and recipient.
Reading or dismissing a notification for one recipient does not mark it read or
dismiss it for another. Definitions specify default enablement, mandatory status,
supported channels, role applicability and retention. User preference changes
apply to subsequent recipient resolution; they are not deletion of old deliveries.
A mandatory definition cannot be disabled. Inactive users are excluded from new
delivery, and their authenticated Work Center requests are denied.

These creation services join an already active unit of work or own a transaction
when none exists. A returned `ChangedUserIds` is not evidence that an enclosing
transaction committed. The application must wait for commit before notifying
clients. The example confirms that an uncommitted/rolled-back notification is
invisible to separate HTTP requests and that the same deduplication key works
after rollback. It sends no email or external messages.

## Transactional document-event projection

The [withdrawal policy](../examples/equipment-inspection/EquipmentInspection.Runtime/InspectionWithdrawalPolicy.cs)
implements `IDocumentActionCompletedWorkCenterPolicy`. In this example, an
inspection's `unpost` event asks its linked actor to review the withdrawal and
sends an informational in-app notification. The task concerns a recorded event;
subsequent posting does not erase that review obligation. A later withdrawal has
a new event ID and produces a separate review. This is example application policy,
not a platform-wide rule. Other document/action types and events without a linked
actor are ignored. Applications requiring supervisor/role assignment must define
that policy explicitly rather than infer a recipient from an administrator token.

Both mutations use the event ID in stable deduplication keys, preserve correlation,
and use the completion event as their causation ID. The policy returns the union
of changed users. It neither starts another transaction nor sends realtime signals
or external messages. Runtime executes all registered policies and marks the claimed
attempt completed inside one transaction. The API explicitly owns polling through
`AddNgbWorkCenterOutboxProcessing`; registering SignalR alone does not start it.
Keep that owner distinct from the example's Hangfire worker.

The [HTTP/outbox cases](../examples/equipment-inspection/EquipmentInspection.IntegrationTests/WorkCenterOutboxTests.cs)
observe the actual dispatcher event, verify both writes inside the projection's
transaction, inject a later policy failure, and confirm separate HTTP reads see
neither item. A subsequent retry commits one task and one notification. Reads from
inside the realtime callback verify that data is already committed. Replaying the
action or applying the same policy event again creates no duplicates. Another case
rolls back a test-owned envelope, then commits the same envelope successfully.
The synthetic envelope isolates persistence behavior; it does not pretend that a
document action occurred. Realtime failure after commit is logged by the SDK and
does not retry or undo the persisted projection; clients can recover through queries.
These tests replace the notifier and do not certify SignalR transport or browser UI.

The [delivery cases](../examples/equipment-inspection/EquipmentInspection.IntegrationTests/OutboxDeliveryTests.cs)
exercise public Runtime and PostgreSQL packages without an API poller. A test clock
advances retry/lease time; the real provider retains state across fresh runtime
service containers. In 3.4.0, the processor claims at most 25 events per call and
dead-letters a persistent failure on attempt eight. Backoff is exponential with
event-specific jitter; do not implement an immediate hot-loop retry. The test
verifies no retry after one second and eventual eligibility after advancing beyond
the supported backoff, without asserting an exact jitter value. Dead-lettered
delivery remains in `FailedCount` but leaves `PendingCount`; zero pending alone
does not mean healthy. Automatic processing does not resume a dead-lettered event
merely because its policy is later fixed. This example exposes no manual redrive API.

Claims are exclusive across concurrent consumers. Abandoned claims become eligible
after the provider's 30-minute lease; the tests advance 31 minutes, reclaim attempt
two, reject completion by attempt one, then complete the current attempt. A fresh
dependency container models processor restart, not a process-kill/host-recovery test.
Health's pending count excludes currently processing leases. Use it with failure
counts and delivery logs; do not treat a momentary zero as proof of full drainage.

## Public pages and realtime delivery

The example registers `NgbWorkCenterPage` at `/work-center` and
`NgbNotificationPreferencesPage` at `/settings/notifications`, using the declared
`@ngbplatform/ui/work-center` entry. These paths match the default navigation
contract. The shell uses `createDefaultNgbWorkCenterConfig` for the authenticated
HTTP gateway and SignalR client. Its proxy forwards `/hubs` with WebSocket support
as well as `/api`; the API maps the existing Work Center hub.

The [browser case](../examples/equipment-inspection/web/tests/e2e/inspection.spec.ts)
withdraws a real inspection in one tab and observes the actual `workCenterChanged`
WebSocket invocation in a second tab. That tab displays the task and notification
without navigation or refresh. It dismisses the notice, snoozes the task, reloads
saved notification preferences, and confirms a second withdrawal still creates a
mandatory review while the optional notice is disabled. Authentication, source
authorization, projection and database writes are real; no HTTP or hub mock feeds
the page. The test records only frame kind/count, never the access-token query in
the socket URL. Transport reconnect, other browsers and responsive layouts remain
separate compatibility cases.

Use this for bootstrap, adding module projects or changing host composition. For

name: ngb-background-jobs

Read [background jobs](../../references/background-jobs.md) before composing a

---
name: ngb-documents
description: Explain standard NGB document posting or implement document definitions, validation, actions and register effects in an application.
---

## Standard Post

Standard Post requires a registered Accounting, OperationalRegisters or
ReferenceRegisters handler. After validation, a handler that emits no records
can move a Draft to `Posted` with no register movements. If all handlers are
absent, automatic registration omits Post. If the application explicitly exposes
the action anyway, executing it returns `doc.posting.handler.not_configured`. The
document stays in `Draft` and its effects stay unchanged.

An empty RR posting handler is not a guaranteed lifecycle callback: Unpost skips
it when the document has no RR write state. Never put dependency guards there.
Read [withdrawal boundaries](../../references/documents.md#withdrawal-and-dependent-documents)
and [visible flow relationships](../../references/documents.md#visible-document-flow).

## Implementing a document

1. Read [document contracts](../../references/documents.md). Inspect the installed
   `NGB.Platform.Definitions` and application definitions, validators and storage.
2. Define head/part metadata and an immutable migration. Keep fields nullable where
   incomplete Drafts are valid; attach business completion checks with
   `AddPostValidator<T>()`, not an unconditional draft check.
   Map `ColumnType.String` to PostgreSQL `text`, including bounded fields; use a
   `CHECK` for the database length limit. `varchar(n)` fails SDK schema validation.
   For bounded text, metadata `MaxLength` does not enforce the Draft HTTP limit.
   Implement both methods of `IDocumentDraftPayloadValidator` in Runtime and
   register it by that interface in DI. Follow the linked reference's
   [payload validation example](../../references/documents.md#draft-text-limits).
3. Choose effects according to the application's business rules. For a workflow
   with no register movements, bind the empty handler in Definitions and register
   its implementation in DI. Let the standard action validate and change status.
4. Route interactive actions through the authorized action dispatcher. Preserve
   idempotency keys, expected versions and the existing action availability rules.
   Reload the version after Draft saves. Check the registry date explicitly:
   generic payload dates are not automatically bound to it in 3.4.0, and generic
   save has no expected-version check. Read the documented limitations first.
5. Test incomplete Draft, invalid Post, valid Post, retry, concurrent change and
   unauthorized action against the actual service/API path. Assert the resulting
   effects and preserved history independently of implementation details.
   For replay, use `InspectionRequests.AssertEquivalentJsonAsync` from the example
   to compare the complete response even when object properties change order.
   When adding a Post requirement, update `CompleteInspectionPayload` and all
   positive setup paths that depend on it, including reports, batch posting and
   typed-storage guards. Preserve explicit incomplete Drafts and frozen migration
   setup; do not fill required fields automatically in generic HTTP/action helpers.
   Validate the migrated physical schema against metadata before lifecycle tests;
   follow [schema validation](../../references/persistence.md#typed-schema-validation-and-posted-document-guards).
6. Run `node infrastructure/ngb.mjs validate --profile build`,
   `node infrastructure/ngb.mjs test` and
   `node infrastructure/ngb.mjs test --profile integration`.

Done means the requested lifecycle and effect outcomes are proven. A validator
unit test alone is not evidence of persistence, authorization or successful Post.
